title: API gateways and edge concerns
subtitle: An API gateway does the shared work for every request at the edge. Learn what belongs there, what does not, and how to stop it taking everything down.

c.v: This is a real incident, retold from Google's official report. Google and Google Cloud APIs are served through an API management layer. For each incoming API request, it checks that the request is authorized and within policy and
The core program that does these checks is called Service Control. It is a regional service, and it sits in the request path of each API call that comes in.

On June 12, 2025, a policy change with blank fields was copied to every region within seconds. A new quota check in Service Control read the blank fields and crashed, again and again, in every region. API requests got 503 errors around the world.

So one shared check, in front of everything, took down many Google Cloud products at once. Engineers found the cause within 10 minutes and finished turning the check off within 40 minutes. One of the larger regions, us-central1, took up to about 2 hours 40 minutes to recover fully.
Among Google's fixes: make Service Control
, so a failing check does not block API requests. And copy global data changes in stages, with time to catch problems.

Without it, every service must do its own
and logging. With it, you do those once, in one place. Microsoft calls this "offloading" shared jobs to the gateway.

Put shared, generic work in the gateway: checks that are the same for every service. Keep business rules in the services. The gateway must be as boring and as reliable as possible, because everything depends on it.
A request passes through the gateway's steps in order. A cheap check that fails stops the request before any expensive work.
The gateway decrypts the request. Microsoft's guidance is to then open a new TLS connection to the backend, not plain HTTP.

Gateway, load balancer or service mesh?
These three overlap, and one product can play several roles. Ask what each one knows.

A mobile app and a desktop website often need different data. One shared backend that serves both gets pulled in two directions.
(BFF) pattern gives each interface its own small backend. Sam Newman says a BFF is usually owned by the same team as the user interface. His guide is "one experience, one BFF".
Expect some duplicated code across BFFs; Microsoft lists that as a likely cost.
Microsoft's worked example puts one gateway in front for shared checks, with a BFF for each client behind it.
Microsoft's advice is short: never offload business logic to the gateway.
If the gateway holds rules for one service, each change to that service can force a gateway redeploy. If the gateway team releases more slowly, it becomes a bottleneck for every other team.
A good test: would this logic be the same for every service? Token checks, yes. "Refunds over ₹10,000 need a manager", no.

Three more traps from the same guide.
If clients can call a backend directly, they skip auth and limits. Let backends accept traffic only from the gateway.
Do not treat an unverified forwarded header as proof of who the caller is. The gateway must also prove its own identity to the backend.
Each hop and each check adds time. Measure it.
Decide in advance what each check does when it fails. Google plans to make Service Control fail open.
Our advice: a broken rate limiter can fail open, but a broken token check must fail closed.

Timeouts and retries at the edge
The gateway gives up on slow services. Envoy's route
defaults to 15 seconds. It covers the wait for the complete response from the service.
On AWS API Gateway, as of October 2026, a REST API's integration timeout is 50 milliseconds to 29 seconds by default. Regional and private APIs can ask for more.
Our advice: set the gateway's timeout a little longer than the service's own timeouts. Otherwise the service keeps working after the client is gone.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: For every new gateway rule, ask:
"Is this the same for every service?"
If not, it goes in the service.
Know what happens when each gateway check fails. Write "fail open" or "fail closed" next to it.
Treat gateway config like code. Review it, test it and roll it out in stages, as Google now plans to do with global data.
Line up timeouts from the outside in: client, then gateway, then service, then database. Each inner one is shorter.
Watch gateway latency and error rate per route. A slow gateway makes every service look slow.
Make sure backends cannot be called around the gateway.
"Read our gateway config. List every route with its upstream, timeout, retry policy and auth rule. Flag any route that retries a POST without an idempotency key."
"Here is a gateway plugin we wrote. Point out any business logic in it that should move into a service, and explain why."
"Write a test plan for our gateway: kill one instance under load, make the token service slow, and send a request with a forged user header. Say what users should see in each case."
The agent did not invent config keys. Check them against the docs for your gateway.

q.v: Which job should NOT live in the API gateway?

options.v: Checking that the access token is valid.
Deciding whether an order can be refunded.
Rejecting clients that send too many requests.

why.v: A refund rule is business logic. It belongs in the orders service, so changing it does not mean changing and redeploying the shared gateway.

q.v: What is the main difference between an API gateway and a service mesh?

options.v: A gateway handles requests coming in from outside; a mesh handles calls between your own services.
A gateway only works over HTTP/1.1.
A mesh replaces the need for TLS.

why.v: The gateway is the front door for clients. A mesh uses proxies, often one next to each service, to manage service-to-service traffic.

q.v: The gateway's route timeout is 15 seconds. The orders service has its own 20 second timeout to the database. What can happen?

options.v: The gateway gives up at 15 seconds, but the service keeps working for a client that has already left.

why.v: Envoy's route timeout ends the wait at the gateway. Inner timeouts should be shorter than outer ones, or work continues after nobody is waiting.

q.v: Your gateway may retry failed upstream calls. Which requests are safe to retry automatically?

options.v: Requests that are idempotent, such as GET, or POST with an idempotency key.
Only requests that timed out after the response started.

why.v: A retry can run the request twice. Only retry when running it twice has the same effect as running it once.

q.v: In June 2025, why did one bad policy record break Google APIs in every region?

options.v: The policy data was copied to all regions within seconds, and every region's check crashed on it.
A single data centre lost power.

why.v: The data spread to every region within seconds, and the new code had no error handling and no feature flag.
